title: God so loved (John 3:16–21)
hook: God so loved the world as to give his only begotten son

segments.voice: Yesterday, anothen: born again and from above, and a wind that blows where it will. Your line was the wind bloweth where it will. Now, a new week.

John 3:16. On a cardboard sign behind the end zone. Printed on the bottom of a fast food cup. Painted under an athlete's eyes. Scribbled on a highway overpass. It turns up everywhere, cut down, over and over, to a chapter and a number. Today we take it off the poster and read it where it actually sits: in the middle of a long night conversation, with Nicodemus, the teacher who came by night, still in the room.
screen: `A SIGN BEHIND THE END ZONE.` → `REDUCED TO A NUMBER.` → `BACK INTO THE NIGHT TALK.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "For God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son; that whosoever believeth in him, may not perish, but may have life everlasting." Start with so. In English we hear so as so much: God loved the world so very much. Some readers point out that the Greek word can also mean in this way, like this. God loved the world like this: by giving. The love is measured by what it gave. Then the world. In John's Gospel, it's the world that, as the prologue says, knew him not. God loves that world. Not a better world. This one. Then gave, and only begotten: some readers hear an echo of Abraham, asked to offer Isaac, his only son, whom he loved. The next line is just as important, and it almost never makes the posters: "For God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world, but that the world may be saved by him." Not to judge. To save. John then speaks of light and darkness: people sometimes prefer the dark, because they don't want their deeds seen, and the one who does truth comes to the light. Something honest to know: John doesn't mark where Jesus's words to Nicodemus end and his own reflection begins, and readers still discuss it. Some Bibles print verse 16 in red, as Jesus speaking; others don't. Either way, the Church reads it at Mass, and the Catechism quotes this line in saying the Word became flesh so that we might know God's love.
screen: `SO: NOT ONLY HOW MUCH, BUT HOW.` · `THE WORLD THAT DIDN'T KNOW HIM.` · `NOT TO JUDGE, BUT TO SAVE.` · `WHERE DO HIS WORDS END?` · then, large: `GOD SO LOVED THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Say the verse slowly in your mind, for God so loved the world, and let the world get smaller: your country, your town, your street, your house, you. Some Christians pray it this way, putting their own name where the world is. If you pray, say it so, for God so loved me; if you don't, just notice what it's like to hear a sentence about love with you inside it.
Houtos. The Greek word for so in John 3:16: not only how much God loved, but how, by giving his only begotten Son. Today's word.
Your line: so loved the world. This world, as it is, with you in it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John 3:16 at Mass on the Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity in one year of the cycle and on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in another, and the Catechism quotes it in explaining why the Word became flesh.

chat.says: What's the line right after John 3:16? I don't think I've ever heard it.
options: God sent not his Son to judge the world, but that the world may be saved by him.
That the Son would stay in heaven and send an angel to the world instead.
That only those who heard Jesus in person would be given life everlasting.
chat.meaning: John 3:17 says God sent not his Son to judge the world, but that the world may be saved by him. Not to judge: to save.
